description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: No One Is Crazy With Their Own Money
cards.subtitle: Your grandmother keeps $40,000 in cash under her bed. She lived through hyperinflation.
body: She watched her parents' savings evaporate overnight. You think she's paranoid. She thinks you're reckless for trusting banks.
People who grew up in crashes hoard cash. People who grew up in booms chase risk.
cards.takeaway: Everyone's relationship with money is shaped by experiences you didn't have.

cards.title: Luck and Skill Are Nearly Impossible to Separate
cards.subtitle: Bill Gates went to Lakeside School. One of three high schools in America with a computer terminal in 1968.
body: He was brilliant. He also won a lottery he didn't know he'd entered. Somewhere there's an equally talented kid who went to a different school.

• Extreme outcomes require extreme luck
• You can't measure the split
• We credit skill for success and poor choices for failure
cards.takeaway: Effort matters. So does admitting you don't control everything.

cards.title: Enough Is a Moving Target That Destroys Wealth
cards.subtitle: Rajat Gupta had $100 million. He committed insider trading to get a little more. He lost everything.
body: Bernie Madoff had billions under management. Respected. Set. He ran a Ponzi scheme for extra returns.
There's no dollar amount that creates the feeling of enough. It's a reflex you build, not a target you hit.
cards.takeaway: Wanting more risks losing what you have.

cards.title: Compounding Doesn't Feel Like It's Working
cards.subtitle: Warren Buffett made $81.5 billion of his $84.5 billion after turning 65. That's 96% of his wealth.
body: He started investing at 10. For decades it looked like steady, unspectacular growth. Then suddenly he became one of the richest people alive.
The first 20 years feel like nothing. The last 20 years contain nearly everything.
cards.takeaway: Patience isn't a virtue here. It's the entire mechanism.

cards.title: Getting Wealthy and Staying Wealthy Are Different Skills
cards.subtitle: You took huge risks to build the business. Now those same instincts are going to blow it up.
body: Getting money requires optimism. Keeping it requires paranoia. These mindsets are opposites.

• The person who's great at accumulation is terrible at preservation
• Boldness builds wealth
• Fear protects it
cards.takeaway: Building and protecting require opposite temperaments.

cards.title: Tails Drive Everything
cards.subtitle: Your VC fund made 50 investments. 47 failed. 2 returned capital. 1 made 100x and salvaged everything.
body: That's how it works. Most venture returns come from a few deals. Most market gains come from a handful of days.
You can be wrong most of the time. The tails are where all the action is.
cards.takeaway: Stay in the game long enough for the outlier to land.

cards.title: Freedom Is the Highest Dividend
cards.subtitle: You made VP. The salary doubled. Your calendar isn't yours anymore.
body: You wanted the promotion. Now you can't take a Tuesday off without three people needing approval.
Money buys options. Time is the option that matters most.
cards.takeaway: The ultimate goal isn't a number—it's waking up and doing what you want.

cards.title: Wealth Is What You Don't See
cards.subtitle: Your neighbor drives a Porsche. He's leveraged to the teeth. The guy in the Honda has $2 million saved.
body: Spending is visible. Wealth is not. The fancy car tells you nothing. The modest house tells you nothing.

• Wealth is the money that didn't get spent
• Rich means current income
• Wealthy means future options
cards.takeaway: You judge net worth by what people buy—which is exactly backward.

cards.title: Save for No Reason
cards.subtitle: You saved for the house, the wedding, the emergency fund. Then your father got sick and needed live-in care.
body: All your savings had labels. None of them said 'surprise catastrophe.' Life doesn't care about your budget categories.
The most powerful savings have no purpose. The future doesn't announce itself.
cards.takeaway: Purposeless money is freedom money.

cards.title: The Reasonable Beats the Rational
cards.subtitle: The optimal strategy is 100% index funds. You panic-sold during the March 2020 crash anyway.
body: Theory doesn't account for your 3am anxiety. The mathematically perfect plan that you can't stick with is worse than the decent plan you can.
Rational ignores emotion. Reasonable includes it.
cards.takeaway: Being slightly wrong in a sustainable way beats being precisely right in a way that breaks you.

cards.title: Your Personal History Shapes Your Risk Tolerance
cards.subtitle: You started investing in 2009. Your friend started in 2000. You think she's paranoid. She thinks you're reckless.
body: Your first decade was a bull run. Hers opened with a crash. Both of you feel rational.
The market you grew up in is your permanent education. Early crashes breed caution. Early booms breed confidence.
cards.takeaway: The gap between generations is memory, not intelligence.

cards.title: Room for Error Is the Only Free Lunch
cards.subtitle: You were fully invested. The market dropped 40%. You had to sell at the bottom to cover expenses.
body: Your friend kept cash. She 'wasted' returns during the bull run. Then she survived the crash and bought the dip.

• Surviving is the prerequisite for compounding
• Margin of safety looks boring
• Until it saves you
cards.takeaway: Fragility is expensive. Survival is free money.

cards.title: You'll Change, So Plan for That
cards.subtitle: At 25 you built a plan to retire at 55 and travel. At 40 you have kids and can't imagine leaving for a month.
body: The person who made the plan isn't the person living with it. At 25 you wanted adventure. At 40 you want stability.
Rigid plans assume you're fixed. You're not. Sunk cost thinking locks you into outdated goals.
cards.takeaway: Build flexibility into the blueprint.

cards.title: Nothing Is Free in Markets
cards.subtitle: Stocks returned 10% annually. You sold during the March 2020 crash. You wanted the returns without the fear.
body: The price of stock returns is volatility, doubt, and stomach-churning drops. That's not a market flaw. That's the admission fee.
Volatility is the cost, not the bug. You don't get the returns without sitting through the fear.
cards.takeaway: Drops aren't fines—they're the ticket price.

cards.title: Pessimists Sound Smart, Optimists Make Money
cards.subtitle: You listened to the analyst predicting a crash. He sounded smart. He's been predicting crashes for 12 years.
body: Say 'the market will crash' and people nod. Say 'things will probably work out' and you sound naive.
But over any long period, the optimists made money and the pessimists sounded smart at dinner parties.
cards.takeaway: Pessimism gets attention because fear is urgent. Optimism gets ignored because progress is boring.

cards.title: Consensus and Compelling Stories Are Danger Signals
cards.subtitle: Everyone agreed housing always goes up. Your barber was flipping condos. The story was perfect. Then 2008 hit.
body: When consensus is total—when nobody disagrees, when the cabbie is trading options—that's the top.

• Bubbles don't form because people can't do math
• They form because stories beat spreadsheets
• When everyone's in, the only move left is out
cards.takeaway: The time to worry is when nobody is worried.

cards.title: The Seduction of Pessimism
cards.subtitle: The market lost 30% in a week. Recovery took three years. Which one got more headlines?
body: A company collapses overnight. A successful company builds value over decades. Destruction is fast and dramatic.
Bad news is loud. Good news is invisible. The asymmetry in speed makes pessimism feel more real.
cards.takeaway: Headlines shape perception more than data.

cards.title: Debt Psychology Changes Behavior
cards.subtitle: You borrowed for the house, the car, the degree. Now every decision runs through a filter: can I afford the monthly payment?
body: Debt doesn't just cost interest—it reshapes how you think about risk. The person without debt can wait out a recession.
Debt buys you something now by selling claims on your future income. The leverage amplifies gains but eliminates flexibility.
cards.takeaway: The psychological cost isn't on the spreadsheet.

cards.title: Expectations Are the Denominator of Happiness
cards.subtitle: You made $500,000 this year. Your peer made $600,000. You feel poor.
body: Your neighbor makes $50,000 and expected $40,000. She feels rich. You hit half a million and feel behind.
Financial satisfaction is what you have divided by what you expect. The denominator is under your control.
cards.takeaway: The easiest way to get rich is wanting less.

cards.title: Money in Relationships Is About Power and Values
cards.subtitle: You make twice what your partner does. Every financial decision becomes a negotiation about who gets to decide.
body: Money isn't just a number—it's power, identity, and values in one package. Who earns more often means who gets final say.

• Savers feel anxious when spenders relax
• Spenders feel controlled when savers budget
• The fights aren't about the money
cards.takeaway: The fights aren't about the money. They're about whose values win.
